I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-21 19:24 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-22T02:24:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 4.797 degrees and its azimuth is 281.419 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 21.168 degrees and its azimuth is 165.801 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 68.58 percent illuminated, 111.684 degrees from the Sun, and 402237.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—very likely.

At 68.6% illuminated, the Moon is a bright waxing gibbous and is easily visible to normal unaided eyesight in daylight when the sky is clear. An altitude of about 21° puts it comfortably above the horizon, though not especially high, and its separation from the Sun—about 112°—means it is far enough away from the Sun’s glare to be practical to look for.

Look roughly south-southeast (azimuth 166°), about two fist-widths above the horizon at arm’s length (21°). Since the Sun is low in the west, avoid looking anywhere near it; facing south-southeast should keep it well out of your field of view.

It may initially look pale or washed out against the bright blue sky, but once you locate it, it should be quite obvious.
